catalog_quote: Mitani (1978) postulates two internal junctures and one stress phoneme in Eastern Lawa words. The long break is denoted with a space / / and the short break is denoted with a dash /-/. Stress is denoted in the usual way with /ˈ/. The long break / / may occur at certain points in an utterance, marking the border of phonological words, e.g. /ʔˈɔk aʔ nɛwm-kaˈnom/ ‘Where do you come from?’ [...] Final syllables are always stressed and minor syllables are always unstressed. Stress is consistent for words and does not change. A minimal contrast of stress rarely occurs, but in non-final position both stressed and unstressed syllables occur: (i) ˈʔa-ˈlɛ ‘seven’ ˈbuŋ-ˈbaŋ ‘butterfly’ (ii) nak-ˈnəⁱŋ ‘pomelo’ ˀbak-ˈˀbuən ‘between’ [p. 17] ... Some Eastern Lawa words are disyllabic and most of these have an unstressed initial syllable. Examples of di-syllabic words: ləˈʔawm ‘water’ ʔaˈmɔih ‘banana’ kuiˈtɛt ‘papaya’ səˈʔəŋ ‘snake’ baˈho ‘pumpkin’ Tri-syllabic Eastern Lawa words less frequent and are usually formed with two unstressed initials. Examples of tri-syllabic words: maʔsaʔˈŋaj ‘afternoon’ [p. 19]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final (major) syllable of the word; the reduced minor syllables of sesquisyllabic words (kə-, mə-, sə-, lə-, ʔə-) are always unstressed. In compounds of two major syllables joined by short juncture the non-final major syllable may also carry stress (ˈʔa-ˈlɛ 'seven') or not (nak-ˈnəⁱŋ 'pomelo'), so a rare minimal stress contrast exists there; stress is otherwise invariant per word. Corroborated first-hand by Mitani 1966 p. 47 (Bo Luang dialect, in Japanese): the minor syllable 'normally has no stress and its vowel is never lengthened' (通例強勢をもたず母音が長められることもない).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the only sub-word gradation is that non-final major syllables in compounds may be stressed or unstressed (examples above).
new_statements.exceptions: Non-final major syllables in disyllabic compounds may be stressed (ˈʔa-ˈlɛ, ˈbuŋ-ˈbaŋ) — a 'rare' minimal stress contrast; otherwise none. Register (creaky/breathy) non-contrastive (§2.4). Rising vs falling contours on stative verbs vs nouns are treated as intonation, not lexical tone (§2.5 p. 18, after Mitani).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word = optional minor syllable(s) + major syllable; junctures / and -). Section is Blok's summary of Mitani 1978 (Cornell PhD) rather than a fresh analysis, but stands in the phonology chapter of Blok's own fieldwork-based grammar of Bo Luang Eastern Lawa.
new_statements.identity_note: Blok 2013 describes the Bo Luang dialect of Eastern Lawa (Ban Bo Luang and 13 other villages, Bo Luang and Bo Sali subdistricts, Hot District, Chiang Mai), i.e. east2330 proper; Mitani 1966 likewise the Bo Luang dialect. Schlatter 1976 (examined, silent on stress) is the La-Up dialect of WESTERN Lawa (west2396), not this language.

sources.note: §2.5 Stress and intonation, pp. 17-18 (pp. 34-35): 'Final syllables are always stressed and minor syllables are always unstressed. Stress is consistent for words and does not change'; minimal stress contrast rare; non-final major syllables may be stressed or unstressed (ˈʔa-ˈlɛ 'seven' vs nak-ˈnəⁱŋ 'pomelo'); no lexical tone, rising/falling contours are intonational (following Mitani 1978).

sources.note: §4.1 pp. 76-77: Eastern Lawa words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, 'an optional minor unstressed syllable followed by a major syllable'; five minor-syllable types (kə-, mə-, sə-, lə-, ʔə-); minor syllable 'unstressed (and non-tonal)'. Reviews Mitani 1978, Lipsius n.d., Diffloth 1979, Shorto 2006 as the only prior phonologies. No explicit stress rule for the major syllable.

sources.note: §1.6 附属音節 (minor syllable), p. 47 [237], read from page scan: 'ラワ語の附属音節はCV型のみであって、CCVやCVCはない。附属音節は自立音節の直前（または稀れに他の附属音節の直前）にしか立たず、通例強勢をもたず母音が長められることもない。その母音音素も基本的には/ə/のみである。' = the minor syllable is CV only, stands only right before a major (independent) syllable, normally carries no stress and its vowel is never lengthened; vowel basically only /ə/. Also p. 43 [233]: vowels of major syllables are lengthened in isolation, sentence-finally or under emphasis. No stress phoneme set up; no rule for words of two major syllables.
